questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about exudate?

options.label: A
options.text: High specific gravity (>1.020) due to high protein content

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Normal vascular permeability

Because of increased vascular permeability, inflammatory edema fluid is a protein-rich exudate with a high specific gravity. The cutoffs for specific gravity (<1.012 for transudates and >1.020 for exudates) illustrate the point but are not clinically useful.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset chest pain and shortness of breath. An electrocardiogram (ECG) shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Also his serum troponin levels are elevated. He has been diagnosed with myocardial infarction. Which of the following cells are central regulators of hemostasis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Endothelial cells

Endothelial cells are central regulators of hemostasis; the balance between the anti-thrombotic and prothrombotic activities of endothelium determines whether thrombus formation, propagation, or dissolution occurs.

questions.stem: Identify the commonest cause of primary hypercoagulability amongst the following?

options.label: B
options.text: Factor V mutation (called the Leiden mutation)

questions.answerText: Factor V mutation (called the Leiden mutation)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Factor V mutation (called the Leiden mutation)

 

 

Inherited causes of hypercoagulability should be considered in young patients (<50 years of age), even when other acquired risk factors are present

 

  1. Factor V mutation (called the Leiden mutation) is due to an altered amino acid residue in factor V and renders it resistant to proteolysis by protein C. It typically presents with recurrent deep venous thrombosis (DVT).
  2. A single-nucleotide substitution (G to A) in the 3′-untranslated region of the prothrombin gene (in 1%–2% of population). It has a nearly 3 fold increased risk for venous thromboses.
  3. Less common primary hypercoagulable states include inherited deficiencies of anti-coagulants such as anti-thrombin III, protein C, or protein S; affected patients typically present with venous thrombosis and recurrent thromboembolism in adolescence or in early adult life.
  4. Elevated levels of homocysteine contribute to arterial and venous thrombosis, as well as to the development of atherosclerosis. Marked elevations of homocysteine may be caused by an inherited deficiency of cystathione β-synthetase.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents to the clinic with a history of recurrent miscarriages and multiple episodes of deep vein thrombosis. Laboratory tests reveal the presence of lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies. Which of the following best characterizes the condition in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Antiphospholipid Syndrome

Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APLA) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies, such as lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies. It is commonly seen in patients with SLE (secondary APLA Syndrome), although it can also occur independently (10 APLA syndrome).  The key features include

 

About other options

 

In APLA, in vitro, the antibodies interfere with phospholipids and thus inhibit coagulation (hence the name lupus anticoagulant, also a misnomer).

The antibodies also frequently provide a false-positive serologic test for syphilis because the antigen in the standard assay for syphilis is embedded in cardiolipin.

questions.stem: Dr Sparsh was experimenting in his laboratory on hemostasis. He found that a molecule “X” which was responsible for platelet activation using G protein coupled receptor called protease activated receptor 1. Identify “X” in the given scenario:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Thrombin

Thrombin acts via protease activating receptor 1 and its inhibitor vorapaxar is used in the treatment of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old pregnant woman at 38 weeks gestation is admitted to the labor and delivery unit in active labor. During labor, she suddenly becomes unresponsive and goes into cardiac arrest. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is initiated immediately. Despite aggressive resuscitative efforts, the patient does not respond, and unfortunately, she passes away. Autopsy findings reveal the presence of squamous cells, vernix caseosa, and fetal debris within the pulmonary vasculature. Which of the following best explains the underlying pathophysiology of this patient's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Amniotic fluid embolism

Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a rare but potentially fatal obstetric emergency that occurs during labor or shortly after delivery. It is characterized by the entry of amniotic fluid components, such as fetal cells, hair, vernix caseosa, and debris, into the maternal circulation. This can trigger an immediate and severe systemic inflammatory response, leading to cardiovascular collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

questions.stem: A 71-year-old male with a history of poorly controlled hypertension due to him being non compliant with medications is brought to the emergency room by his family because of increasing shortness of breath. An X-ray of the chest reveals bilateral pleural effusions and enlargement of the heart. Given these features, of the following, which is the most likely causative mechanism for the condition producing his shortness of breath?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Increased hydrostatic pressure

Congestive heart failure will increase hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary vasculature, causing fluid to leak into the surrounding space.

questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old female presents to the clinic with complaints of persistent swelling in her right arm following a radical mastectomy for breast cancer. The surgery was performed six months ago, and the patient has been undergoing adjuvant therapy since then. Physical examination reveals significant edema and thickening of the right arm, and the skin over the affected area appears erythematous and indurated. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's arm swelling?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Lymphedema

Postmastectomy edema (also known as postmastectomy lymphedema) is a common complication following radical mastectomy for breast cancer. It is characterized by persistent swelling in the arm on the side of the mastectomy, typically occurring several months to years after the surgery. The removal of lymph nodes disrupts the normal lymphatic drainage of the arm. Salient features of postmastectomy edema include:

 

About other options:

  1. Cellulitis: Cellulitis can cause localized swelling, erythema, and induration of the skin.
  2. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT): DVT can cause unilateral arm swelling, but it is usually associated with pain, warmth, and tenderness in the affected limb. Physical examination and imaging studies would be necessary to confirm the diagnosis of DVT.
  3. Axillary vein stenosis: Axillary vein stenosis can lead to venous outflow obstruction, resulting in arm swelling. However, it is not a common complication following mastectomy.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male Harish Kumar with a history of atrial fibrillation presents to the emergency department with acute-onset left leg pain and swelling. The patient has been non-compliant with anticoagulant therapy for the past few weeks. On physical examination, the left lower extremity appears erythematous and edematous, with palpable cords along the superficial veins. Duplex ultrasonography confirms the presence of a thrombus in the left popliteal vein. Which of the following best represents the components of Virchow triad that contribute to the development of the patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Endothelial injury, platelet aggregation and venous stasis

options.label: B
options.text: Endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and arterial spasm

options.label: C
options.text: Hypercoagulability, venous stasis, and endothelial injury

options.label: D
options.text: Platelet aggregation, arterial spasm, and hypercoagulability

questions.answerText: Hypercoagulability, venous stasis, and endothelial injury
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Hypercoagulability, venous stasis, and endothelial injury

Virchow triad is a set of three factors that contribute to the development of venous thrombosis

questions.stem: Which of the following is the protein is involved in the development of arterial and venous thrombosis in patient with elevated levels of homocysteine?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Fibrinogen

The prothrombotic effects of homocysteine may be due to thioester linkages formed between homocysteine metabolites and a variety of proteins, including fibrinogen.

questions.stem: A young female Basanti presents with recurrent thromboses, repeated miscarriages, cardiac valve vegetations, and thrombocytopenia. Laboratory tests reveal the presence of lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies in the blood. Which of the following is the most plausible explanation for her recurrent fetal loss?

options.label: A
options.text: Antibody mediated thrombocytopenia leading to excessive bleeding

options.label: B
options.text: Antibody mediated thrombosis of placental vessels

options.label: C
options.text: Antibody mediated interference with differentiation of trophoblasts

questions.answerText: Antibody mediated interference with differentiation of trophoblasts
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Antibody mediated interference with differentiation of trophoblasts

 

 

APLA can have multiple manifestations pulmonary embolism (following lower extremity venous thrombosis), pulmonary hypertension (from recurrent subclinical pulmonary emboli), stroke, bowel infarction, or renovascular hypertension depending on vascular bed involved. 

 

Fetal loss does NOT not appear to be caused by thrombosis, but rather seems to stem from antibody-mediated interference with the growth and differentiation of trophoblasts, leading to a failure of placentation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Antibody-mediated thrombocytopenia leading to excessive bleeding

 

  • APS can be associated with thrombocytopenia.
  • But fetal loss is not due to bleeding or low platelets.
  • APS is a hypercoagulable state, not a hemorrhagic one.

 

Option B. Antibody-mediated thrombosis of placental vessels

 

  • Previously accepted mechanism, but Robbins now clarifies this is not the primary reason for fetal loss.
  • While thrombosis can occur, especially in other organs, the fetal loss is mainly due to placental insufficiency from failed trophoblast development.

 

Option D. Antibody-mediated cardiac dysfunction

 

  • APS may cause Libman-Sacks endocarditis, but this does not directly cause fetal loss.
  • Cardiac issues are part of systemic manifestations, not reproductive ones.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th edition, page 128

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of congestive heart failure presents with abdominal pain, ascites, and lower extremity edema. Laboratory tests reveal elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin. Imaging studies show hepatomegaly with a mottled appearance on the liver surface. Liver biopsy demonstrates centrilobular congestion, hemorrhage, and fibrosis. Which of the following best describes the most likely cause of the liver findings in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Nutmeg liver

Nutmeg liver, also known as congestive hepatopathy, is a liver pathology associated with chronic passive congestion due to right-sided heart failure or obstruction of the hepatic veins (Budd-Chiari syndrome). It is called nutmeg liver because the appearance of the liver on cross-section resembles a nutmeg seed due to the centrilobular congestion and peripheral sparing.

In this patient's case, the clinical presentation of abdominal pain, ascites, and lower extremity edema, along with the imaging findings of hepatomegaly with a mottled appearance on the liver surface, are characteristic of nutmeg liver. The elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin can occur as a result of hepatic congestion and impaired liver function in the setting of right-sided heart failure.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male undergoes a central venous catheter insertion for intravenous access during a surgical procedure. Shortly after the catheter insertion, the patient develops sudden-onset dyspnea, tachycardia, and hypotension. Physical examination reveals “mill-wheel” murmur over the precordium. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Air embolism 

 

Clinical Scenario Recap:

 

  • Procedure: Central venous catheter (CVC) insertion
  • Onset: Sudden
  • Symptoms: Dyspnea, tachycardia, hypotension
  • Exam Finding: “Mill-wheel” murmur — a classic hallmark

 

Why it’s Air Embolism:

 

  • Air embolism is a known complication of CVC insertion, especially when:
    • The patient is upright or hypovolemic
    • Proper technique is not followed (e.g., not occluding the catheter hub)
       
  • Pathophysiology: Air enters the venous circulation → reaches the right heart → causes obstruction to pulmonary blood flow.
     
  • Mill-wheel murmur = churning, splashing sound from air-blood interface in the right heart – highly characteristic.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pulmonary embolism: Can cause similar symptoms but not typically associated with mill-wheel murmur or directly after CVC insertion.

 

Option C. Pneumothorax: May follow CVC insertion, especially via subclavian vein, but usually presents with unilateral decreased breath sounds, not a murmur.

 

Option D. Atelectasis: Can cause hypoxia, but not sudden hypotension or murmur; typically a gradual complication.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of a mill-wheel murmur strongly points to air embolism, especially following central venous access procedures.
